proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1999 dissertation Emma LaRocque recommends Miller's Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) as an overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Métis land loss. She also cites 'Miller' with Frideres, Ponting, Dickason and Green for the point that colonial forces acting on Native peoples in Canada were institutional rather than military.
proposed_edges.map_label: Cited by LaRocque as overview and authority, 1999
proposed_edges.evidence_note: LaRocque, Native Writers Resisting Colonizing Practices in Canadian Historiography and Literature (PhD, University of Manitoba, 1999), University of Manitoba repository PDF, read 2026-10-31 at the passages concerned and re-checked by independent review (text layer; OCR slips corrected). PDF p. 56, n. 15: 'For a good overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Metis loss of lands see Frideres, Aboriginal Peoples in Canada; Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens; Dickason, Canada's First Nations.' PDF p. 133: the colonial forces 'have not been military, as a rule, but rather, have been institutional through economic, religious, educational legislative, and media systems (Frideres, Ponting, Miller, Dickason, Green)'. That parenthetical gives no title. Her bibliography lists both 'Miller, J.R. Skyscrapers hide the heavens' (1989) and Christine Miller and Patricia Chuchryk, eds., Women of the First Nations (1997). Reading the p. 133 'Miller' as J. R. Miller is an inference from its context and from n. 15. This is a recommended overview and a citation in argument, not an endorsement of Miller's whole interpretation. LaRocque elsewhere criticises settler 'cross-cultural' historians (her edges to Van Kirk, Brown and Trigger), and Miller is not among those she names there. No Miller text read.

review.reason: Verified in the University of Manitoba repository PDF. PDF p. 56, n. 15: 'For a good overview of treaties, the Indian Act, reserves, residential schools and Metis loss of lands see Frideres, Aboriginal Peoples in Canada; Miller, Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens; Dickason, Canada's First Nations'. PDF p. 133: colonial forces 'have not been military, as a rule, but rather, have been institutional through economic, religious, educational legislative, and media systems (Frideres, Ponting, Miller, Dickason, Green)'. Direction is right: Miller's work feeds LaRocque's argument, so Miller → LaRocque. Judgement on the researcher's question: a recommended-overview footnote and a five-name parenthetical are a thin but real citation-in-argument, not topic overlap. They are worth an edge because they show LaRocque using Miller as an authority while criticising other settler historians, and Miller has only two edges. The wording must be weaker than 'names Miller among the authorities for her argument', and the namesake risk must be recorded. Her bibliography also lists Christine Miller (co-editor of Women of the First Nations, 1997, which contains a LaRocque essay). The p. 133 parenthetical gives no title, so attributing it to J. R. Miller is an inference from context and from n. 15. The 'printed p. 130 by the page offset' claim cannot be checked (printed numbers are not in the text layer); cite PDF pages only.
